case_title: Krishika Lulla & Ors. v. Shyam Vithalrao Devkatia & Anr.
statutory_provisions: Copyright Act 1957 s.63; IPC s.406, s.420 (read with s.34)
evidence_type: None taken at trial; the Court decided only whether the complaint was tenable on the pleaded facts (title copyright)
trial_court_outcome: Cognizance taken and process issued against four accused; no verdict or sentence (complaint stage)
high_court_outcome: Single Judge dismissed the s.482 Cr.P.C. applications and refused to quash the complaint and process
neutral_facts: The complainant states that he wrote a short synopsis of a story titled "Desi Boys" and had it registered with a film writers' association on 25.11.2008. In October 2009 he emailed the synopsis to a friend, who was seeking a comedy film story for the son of a film director. The friend forwarded the synopsis by email to another person, describing it as just an idea, on 15.10.2009. The friend received no reply. Later the complainant saw promotional material for a film titled "Desi Boyz". He alleges that this title infringes copyright in his title. He has not seen the film and cannot say whether any part of his story was used. The accused state that their film was released on 25.11.2011 and was based on a story written by another author under a written agreement dated 02.09.2009 and paid for by cheque. Shooting began on 07.11.2010. The complainant learned of the film around 12.10.2011. The defence details were not examined, as the matter turned on whether the complaint was tenable.
number_of_offences: 3 charged (Copyright Act s.63; IPC s.406; IPC s.420); 0 finally upheld
motive: alleged: adoption of the title "Desi Boyz" for the film infringed the complainant's copyright in the title "Desi Boys"
key_evidence_accepted: The Court relied on the nature of the claim (copyright only in the title) and the title's content; it did not rely on any trial evidence.
witness_credibility: Not applicable; no witnesses assessed. The Court noted the complainant admittedly had not seen the film.
trial_duration: offence: not given; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 22.03.2012; Supreme Court: 15.10.2015
legal_representation: Accused (appellants): Raju Ramachandran, Sr. Adv., with Chirag M. Shroff and others. Respondents: Ramsuresh Vishwakarma, Rajiv Kumar Sinha and others; Respondent No.1 appeared in person. No State counsel is recorded.
investigation_status: Private complaint filed; process issued by Metropolitan Magistrate; no police investigation or charge sheet described
procedural_irregularity: The High Court did not decide the issues raised, observing only that the facts alleged could be determined at trial
appeal_history: Trial court (Metropolitan Magistrate): cognizance taken and process issued. High Court: s.482 applications dismissed on 22.03.2012. Supreme Court: appeals allowed and complaint quashed.
prosecution_argument: The complainant argued that the s.482 applications were rightly dismissed because the defence facts depend on evidence to be led at trial
defence_argument: No copyright subsists in a title, so no complaint under s.63 is tenable; the appellants' story was bought from an author and the films bear no similarity to the synopsis
legal_principle_applied: Under s.13 of the Copyright Act a title is not an original literary work and cannot attract copyright; a complaint for copyright infringement based on a title is not tenable
precedent_relied_upon: Francis Day & Hunter v. Twentieth Century Fox, AIR 1940 PC 55 (relied on); E.M. Forster v. A.N. Parasuram, AIR 1964 Mad 331; Kanungo Media v. RGV Film Factory, (2007) ILR 1 Delhi 1122; R. Radha Krishnan v. A.R. Murugadoss, 2013-5-L.W. 429 (approved); Hogg v. Maxwell (1866-67) LR 2 Ch App 307 (referred to)
other_sentence_order: Criminal Case No. SW/332 of 2011 quashed
